title: Famous Buildings in The Hague: From the Binnenhof to the Peace Palace
description: A guide to The Hague's most famous buildings — the medieval Binnenhof, Peace Palace, Mauritshuis, and Richard Meier's modern City Hall.
body_html:
The Hague's most famous buildings tell the story of a city that governs without being a capital. The Binnenhof, the medieval castle courtyard where Dutch parliament has met for centuries; the Peace Palace, purpose-built home of international law; the Mauritshuis, a jewel-box of Dutch Classicism holding Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring; and Richard Meier's gleaming white City Hall, nicknamed the Ice Palace — together they span some eight centuries of architecture in one compact, walkable center.

Den Haag (as the Dutch call it) is the seat of government, home of the royal court, and host to the International Court of Justice, yet Amsterdam remains the constitutional capital. That in-between status shaped its architecture: stately rather than showy, international rather than merely national. Here are the buildings that define it.

The Binnenhof: Eight Centuries of Dutch Government

The Binnenhof ("inner court") is often described as one of the oldest parliament sites in the world still in use. Begun in the thirteenth century as a castle of the counts of Holland, it grew into a walled complex of halls, gates, and towers around a central courtyard, beside the Hofvijver pond whose reflection provides the city's defining postcard view.

At its heart stands the Ridderzaal, the Knights' Hall, a thirteenth-century Gothic hall with twin turrets and a great timber roof, where the monarch delivers the annual speech from the throne on Prinsjesdag each September. Around it cluster centuries of additions — including the little tower, het Torentje, that serves as the prime minister's office. For the vocabulary of pointed arches and rib vaults on display here, see our Gothic style guide. The complex has been undergoing a major long-term renovation, so check access arrangements before visiting.

The Peace Palace: Architecture for International Law

No building expresses The Hague's identity like the Peace Palace, opened in 1913 to house the Permanent Court of Arbitration and today also home to the International Court of Justice, the principal judicial organ of the United Nations. Funded largely by a gift from the Scottish-American steel magnate Andrew Carnegie, it was designed by French architect Louis Cordonnier following an international competition, in a romantic Neo-Renaissance manner with a landmark clock tower.

The palace is a built diplomatic project: nations around the world donated materials and artworks — gates, marbles, stained glass, and furnishings — so the interior reads as a museum of goodwill. Set in gardens behind wrought-iron gates, it is best appreciated from the visitors' center when the courts are sitting. Outside the gates burns the World Peace Flame, ringed by stones contributed from scores of countries — a small monument that distills the building's entire purpose into a single gesture.

The Mauritshuis: Dutch Classicism in Miniature

Beside the Binnenhof pond stands the Mauritshuis, built in the 1630s–1640s as a residence for Johan Maurits of Nassau-Siegen and designed in the circle of Jacob van Campen and Pieter Post — the same milieu that produced Amsterdam's Royal Palace. It is Dutch Classicism at its most perfect: a compact sandstone block with giant pilasters, crisp pediment, and ideal proportions that architects still study.

Since the nineteenth century it has served as the Royal Picture Gallery, and its small rooms hold an outsized share of Golden Age masterpieces: Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring and View of Delft, Rembrandt's The Anatomy Lesson of Dr Nicolaes Tulp, and Fabritius's The Goldfinch. Few buildings in Europe pack so much art and architecture into so few square meters.

Richard Meier's City Hall: The Ice Palace

The Hague's modern era announced itself in the 1990s with a new City Hall and public library complex by the American architect Richard Meier, master of luminous white modernism. Its vast glass-roofed atrium — among the largest civic halls of its kind in Europe — earned the building its nickname, the IJspaleis or Ice Palace. Love it or find it chilly, it gave the government quarter a confident contemporary heart, and it anchors a downtown skyline that has since grown a cluster of ministry towers by international firms.

Meier's building repays a visit even for skeptics of white modernism. The atrium works as a genuine indoor public square — home to exhibitions, markets, and the city library — and its gridded galleries frame constantly shifting views of people crossing bridges overhead. In a city of closed courtyards and guarded palaces, a government building this transparent was itself a political statement, and residents have gradually made it their own.

More Landmarks: The Passage, the Kurhaus, and the Royal Court

Three more stops round out any architectural walk. The Passage, a glass-roofed shopping arcade from the 1880s, is the Netherlands' surviving nineteenth-century arcade in the grand Parisian mold. Noordeinde Palace, the monarch's working palace, presents a dignified classical face to one of the city's most elegant shopping streets. And by the sea in Scheveningen, the Kurhaus — a grand seaside hotel of the 1880s with a domed concert hall — recalls the era when The Hague's beach resort drew Europe's fashionable classes.

Art lovers should also seek out the Lange Voorhout, a lime-shaded avenue of eighteenth-century mansions that ranks among the most elegant streets in the Netherlands. One of its palaces, once a royal residence, now houses Escher in Het Paleis, a museum devoted to the impossible geometries of M. C. Escher — a fitting tenant for a city that balances so carefully between tradition and invention. A short tram ride away, the Kunstmuseum Den Haag, completed in the 1930s to designs by H. P. Berlage, pairs one of the world's great Mondrian collections with the last major work of the architect who fathered modern Dutch architecture.

Walking It Yourself

The Hague's landmarks sit unusually close together: Binnenhof, Mauritshuis, Noordeinde, and the Passage are minutes apart on foot, with the Peace Palace a pleasant walk through embassy streets and the Kurhaus a tram ride to the sea. For a full itinerary — including where to catch the Hofvijver reflection at golden hour — see our city guide to Den Haag.

The Hague proves that a city's fame need not rest on height or spectacle. Its greatest buildings are rooms where things are decided — a medieval hall, a court of nations, a white atrium — and eight centuries on, the deciding continues.
